patient.chief_complaint: Painful vision loss in the left eye over five days
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Amara Osei is a 26-year-old right-handed African American woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a five-day history of progressive vision loss in her left eye accompanied by pain behind the eye that worsens with eye movement. She reports that five days ago she began noticing blurring and fogginess in her left visual field while studying on her laptop, which she initially attributed to eye strain and fatigue. By the following morning the vision had worsened considerably, and she noticed that colors appeared washed out, particularly reds, which looked brownish through the left eye. She also developed a dull aching pain behind the left eye that became sharper with lateral and upward gaze movements, rating it a 6 out of 10 at worst. Over the next three days, the vision in her left eye deteriorated to the point where she could only perceive hand motions centrally, prompting her roommates to bring her to the emergency department. She reports that her symptoms seem to worsen after hot showers, with the vision becoming even more blurred for 30 to 60 minutes after exposure to heat. On further directed questioning, she recalls that approximately eight months ago she had a two-to-three week episode of tingling and numbness involving the right side of her trunk and right arm in a hemibody distribution. She saw her university health center at the time and was told the numbness was likely stress-related; it resolved spontaneously without treatment. She did not seek further evaluation. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, weakness, ataxia, bowel or bladder dysfunction, or speech difficulty. She denies recent fevers, weight loss, rash, oral ulcers, joint pains, or other systemic symptoms. She denies recent viral illness or vaccinations. She has no history of foreign travel. She is currently in her second year of her PhD program and had been under increased academic stress over the past several weeks.

results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria
results.authors: Thompson AJ, Banwell BL, Barkhof F, et al.
results.key_finding: The 2017 McDonald criteria revised the rules for clinically isolated syndrome (CIS): when DIS is demonstrated by MRI, CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (not present in paired serum) may substitute for dissemination in time (DIT), permitting an MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack. Symptomatic lesions may also be used to establish DIS.

results.title: MRI criteria for the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: MAGNIMS consensus guidelines
results.authors: Filippi M, Rocca MA, Ciccarelli O, et al.
results.key_finding: Dissemination in space (DIS) requires at least one T2 lesion in at least 2 of 4 CNS areas: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord. Optic nerve lesions contributing to DIS are supported by MRI and VEP.

results.title: Multiple sclerosis
results.authors: Reich DS, Lucchinetti CF, Calabresi PA.
results.key_finding: Optic neuritis is the presenting feature in approximately 20-25% of MS patients. The McDonald 2017 OCB substitution for DIT allows MS diagnosis at the time of a first demyelinating attack when DIS is met, enabling earlier DMT initiation and potentially reducing disability accumulation.

output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time when dissemination in space is established by MRI. This permits an MS diagnosis after a single clinical attack (CIS), avoiding the need to wait for a second clinical relapse. DIS requires T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 characteristic CNS regions. The substitution rule applies only when OCBs are CSF-restricted (absent in paired serum).

output.proposed: Ocrelizumab 300 mg IV (two infusions 2 weeks apart, then 600 mg every 6 months); or dimethyl fumarate 120 mg twice daily for 7 days then 240 mg twice daily
interactions: Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol/norethindrone): No significant pharmacokinetic interaction with ocrelizumab. No interaction with dimethyl fumarate.
Albuterol inhaler: No interaction with ocrelizumab or dimethyl fumarate.
contraindications: Ocrelizumab: Contraindicated in patients with active HBV infection (screen HBsAg and anti-HBc before initiation). Contraindicated in active severe infection.
Dimethyl fumarate: Contraindicated in patients with severe lymphopenia (lymphocytes <0.5 x10^9/L).
warnings: Ocrelizumab: Screen for hepatitis B virus before initiation (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs); reactivation risk in carriers.
Ocrelizumab: Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation; ensure immunizations are up to date at least 4-6 weeks prior to first infusion.
Ocrelizumab: Infusion-related reactions common (hypotension, bronchospasm); premedicate with methylprednisolone, antihistamine, and antipyretic 30 minutes prior.
Ocrelizumab: Monitor for PML, though risk is substantially lower than with natalizumab; JCV serostatus is not a contraindication.
Dimethyl fumarate: GI side effects (flushing, nausea, diarrhea) common in first month; take with food to reduce flushing.
Dimethyl fumarate: Monitor CBC including lymphocyte count before initiation and every 6 months; withhold if lymphocytes persistently <0.5 x10^9/L for >6 months (PML risk).
All DMTs in women of childbearing potential: Discuss contraception and family planning before initiation; natalizumab and ocrelizumab have limited safety data in pregnancy.
Natalizumab: JCV serostatus required before initiation; PML risk substantially elevated in JCV-seropositive patients with index >0.9 and prior immunosuppressant use.
output.formulary_status: Ocrelizumab: formulary, prior authorisation required for the labelled indication. Dimethyl fumarate: formulary, preferred oral agent in this class.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain contrast-enhanced brain MRI with MS protocol (FLAIR, T2, DWI, pre- and post-gadolinium T1, fat-saturated T2 through orbits) to assess dissemination in space and active optic neuritis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Multifocal T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial); enhancing left optic nerve confirming active optic neuritis; all white matter lesions non-enhancing — MRI alone does not establish DIT because no simultaneous enhancing + non-enhancing white matter lesions are present

optimal_actions.action: Extend MRI to cervical and thoracic spinal cord with contrast — cord involvement counts toward DIS and distinguishes MS from NMOSD
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies) peripheral cord lesion at C5-C6, non-enhancing — adds the fourth MS region (spinal cord) to established DIS (periventricular + juxtacortical + infratentorial already present on brain MRI); absence of longitudinally extensive myelitis argues against NMOSD

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis including oligoclonal bands (with paired serum), IgG index, cell count, protein, and glucose
optimal_actions.expected_finding: CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands absent in paired serum) are present — this is the load-bearing finding that satisfies DIT under McDonald 2017 OCB-for-DIT rule, establishing full RRMS diagnosis at first attack; IgG index elevated, mild lymphocytic pleocytosis

optimal_actions.action: Order mimic-exclusion serology: CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, vitamin D, ANA, AQP4-IgG (cell-based assay), MOG-IgG (cell-based assay), HIV, and RPR
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG negative — excludes NMOSD and MOGAD; B12, TSH, HIV, RPR, ANA negative — excludes other mimics; low vitamin D is a recognised MS risk factor and modifiable comorbidity but does not explain the demyelinating presentation

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis or relapse characterization; findings are non-specific and add no information about demyelination.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for visualizing demyelinating plaques and the optic nerve; adds radiation without clinical benefit in this presentation.
No cardiac indication exists in this presentation; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod bradyarrhythmia monitoring — not as part of MS diagnostic workup in a patient without cardiac symptoms.
FDG-PET is not indicated in MS diagnosis or DMT decision-making; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and adds substantial cost without clinical benefit.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard pre-LP safety imaging: confirm absence of mass effect or elevated intracranial pressure on brain MRI before performing lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Apply McDonald 2017 criteria: with DIS established across ≥3 MS-typical regions (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord on follow-up MRI), plus CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands satisfying the OCB-for-DIT substitution rule, the diagnosis is RRMS — not 'CIS pending a second attack'
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays (not ELISA) before committing to an MS diagnosis and initiating DMT
Treat acute optic neuritis relapse with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days to hasten visual recovery; plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe visual loss
Initiate disease-modifying therapy after relapse stabilization; discuss high-efficacy vs. platform approach, reproductive plans, HBV screening, and JCV serostatus
Screen for hepatitis B (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) before initiating ocrelizumab or other B-cell depleting therapies
Counsel the patient that she has RRMS — not a 'syndrome awaiting a second event' — and that early DMT reduces long-term disability accumulation
contraindicated_actions: Do not defer the MS diagnosis or DMT initiation on the grounds that this is 'only a first attack'; McDonald 2017 DIS + CSF OCBs establish RRMS at this encounter — waiting for a second clinical relapse is not required and exposes the patient to avoidable relapses
Do not diagnose NMOSD without confirming AQP4-IgG positivity by cell-based assay — the short-segment cord lesion and brain lesion distribution are atypical for NMOSD
Do not use an ELISA-based AQP4 or MOG antibody assay — unacceptable false-negative rates; cell-based assays are required
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring (4–6 hour observation)
Do not start teriflunomide or cladribine without confirmed effective contraception — both are teratogenic with prolonged effects
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiating B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators
key_reasoning_points: The clinical picture is a first demyelinating attack (acute left optic neuritis); the naive conclusion that this is 'CIS — not yet MS' and that a second attack is required before diagnosis is the primary red herring to avoid

McDonald 2017 introduced the OCB-for-DIT substitution rule: when DIS is met and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands absent in paired serum) are present, DIT is satisfied without a second clinical attack or follow-up MRI — this patient meets RRMS criteria at first presentation

DIS is satisfied here by involvement of ≥3 of 4 MS-typical MRI regions: periventricular (four lesions), juxtacortical (left parietal), infratentorial (dorsal pons) — confirmed from brain MRI alone, with spinal cord added on follow-up

The brain MRI lacks simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing white matter lesions — the only enhancing focus is the optic nerve (the symptomatic lesion); MRI alone therefore does NOT establish DIT, making the CSF OCB finding load-bearing
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be sent as cell-based assays; both are negative, excluding NMOSD and MOGAD before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT
Low vitamin D (18 ng/mL despite supplementation) is a recognised MS risk factor and modifiable comorbidity; it does NOT explain the presentation and should not divert the diagnostic workup

red_herrings.data_point: Single clinical demyelinating attack (first-ever acute optic neuritis) with no prior documented neurological event
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent to conclude this is 'CIS — wait for a second attack before diagnosing MS', applying the pre-2017 McDonald framework rather than the revised 2017 criteria
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: McDonald 2017 permits RRMS diagnosis after a single clinical attack when DIS is met on MRI and CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands substitute for DIT; a second attack is not required

red_herrings.data_point: Low vitamin D, 25-hydroxy 18 ng/mL (below reference 30-100 ng/mL) — worse despite ongoing supplementation
red_herrings.intended_effect: May tempt the agent to attribute the patient's optic symptoms to a metabolic or nutritional aetiology, or to emphasise vitamin D supplementation as the primary intervention
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Low vitamin D is a recognised MS risk factor and modifiable comorbidity, not a cause of acute optic neuritis; supplementation is appropriate but does not change the demyelinating diagnosis or alter the need for DMT
